question: When may you use hazard warning lights while your vehicle is moving?
options: On a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway, to warn following drivers of a hazard ahead
When driving slowly looking for an address
When being towed in any circumstances
When double-parked for a short time
explanation: Hazard warning lights. These may be used when your vehicle is stationary, to warn that it is temporarily obstructing traffic. Never use them as an excuse for dangerous or illegal parking. You MUST NOT use hazard warning lights while driving or being towed unless you are on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway and you need to warn drivers behind you of a hazard or obstruction ahead. (Highway Code rule 116.)

question: You see road humps and chicanes ahead. What are they designed to do?
options: Test your suspension
Separate cycle and motor traffic
Allow water to drain from the road
Slow traffic down
explanation: Traffic-calming measures. On some roads there are features such as road humps, chicanes and narrowings intended to slow you down. Reduce your speed when you see them. (Highway Code rule 153.)

question: You want to overtake a long, slow lorry on a busy road. What should you do first?
options: Sound your horn before pulling out
Drop back so you can see further ahead and the lorry driver can see you
Move up close so you can pull out quickly
Flash your headlights so the lorry moves over
explanation: Large vehicles. Overtaking these is more difficult. Drop back to increase your ability to see ahead and to allow the driver of the large vehicle to see you in their mirrors. (Highway Code rule 164.)

question: In which of these places does the Highway Code say you should NOT overtake because you cannot see far enough ahead?
options: On a long straight dual carriageway
Approaching the brow of a hill
When the vehicle in front signals left
On a 30 mph road
explanation: DO NOT overtake if there is any doubt, or where you cannot see far enough ahead to be sure it is safe — for example when you are approaching a corner or bend, a hump bridge, or the brow of a hill. (Highway Code rule 166.)

question: You see a flashing amber light beneath a school warning sign. What does it mean?
options: No vehicles allowed during school hours
Stop and wait for the light to go out
School crossing patrol is not on duty
Children may be crossing the road ahead — slow down
explanation: Near schools. Drive slowly and be particularly aware of young cyclists and pedestrians. In some places, there may be a flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign which tells you that there may be children crossing the road ahead. (Highway Code rule 208.)

question: Why are motorcyclists and cyclists particularly hard to see at junctions?
options: They always travel in the middle of the lane
They are easily hidden by other vehicles and may be filtering through traffic
They are required to ride on the pavement
They never use lights
explanation: It is often difficult to see motorcyclists and cyclists, especially when they are coming up from behind, coming out of junctions, at roundabouts, overtaking you or filtering through traffic. Always look out for them before you emerge from a junction. (Highway Code rule 211.)

question: You are following a large articulated lorry. Why should you keep well back?
options: Lorries can stop more quickly than cars
It is illegal to be within two car lengths of a lorry
You will save fuel
The driver may not be able to see you in their mirrors
explanation: Large vehicles may need extra road space to turn or to deal with a hazard that you are not able to see. If you are following a large vehicle, such as a bus or articulated lorry, be aware that the driver may not be able to see you in their mirrors. (Highway Code rule 221.)

question: A vehicle ahead is showing a flashing amber beacon. What does this indicate?
options: A doctor on an emergency call
A slow-moving or stationary vehicle, or an abnormal load — approach with caution
A police vehicle on patrol
A vehicle that has broken down and must not be passed
explanation: Vehicles with flashing amber beacons. These warn of a slow-moving or stationary vehicle (such as a traffic officer vehicle, salt spreader, snow plough or recovery vehicle) or abnormal loads, so approach with caution. On unrestricted dual carriageways, motor vehicles first used on or after 1 January 1947 with a maximum speed of 25 mph or less MUST use a flashing amber beacon. (Highway Code rule 225.)

question: You are about to overtake a cyclist on a windy day near a gap in a hedge. Why should you allow extra room?
options: It is a legal requirement on windy days
They may stop without warning
They may turn right
A sudden gust could blow them off course
explanation: Windy weather. High-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course. This can happen on open stretches of road exposed to strong crosswinds, or when passing bridges or gaps in hedges. (Highway Code rule 232.)

question: After a long dry spell it starts to rain. Why might the road surface be especially slippery?
options: The tyres have hardened in the heat
The brakes have absorbed moisture
Oil and rubber deposits on the surface mix with the rain
Rain neutralises the road salt
explanation: Hot weather. Keep your vehicle well ventilated to avoid drowsiness. Be aware that the road surface may become soft or if it rains after a dry spell it may become slippery. If you are dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and if necessary, stop. (Highway Code rule 237.)

question: At road works a temporary speed limit is displayed. What does this mean?
options: It applies only to HGVs
It is mandatory — you MUST NOT exceed it
It applies only when workers are visible
It is advisory only
explanation: When the 'Road Works Ahead' sign is displayed, take extra care and look for additional signs providing more specific instructions. You MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit. Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front. (Highway Code rule 288.)

question: You are crossing a level crossing when the amber light comes on. What should you do?
options: Reverse off the crossing
Sound your horn and accelerate
Keep going — do not stop on the crossing
Stop immediately
explanation: Controlled Crossings. Most crossings have traffic light signals with a steady amber light, twin flashing red stop lights and an audible alarm. You MUST always obey the flashing red stop lights. You MUST stop behind the white line across the road. Keep going if you have already crossed the white line when the amber light comes on. (Highway Code rule 293.)

question: Why should you take extra care where trams operate?
options: Trams move quietly and cannot steer to avoid you
Trams travel faster than other traffic
Tram tracks are always electrified
Trams always have right of way over pedestrians
explanation: Tramways. You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams. Take extra care where trams run along the road. The width taken up by trams is often shown by tram lanes marked by white lines, yellow dots or by a different type of road surface. (Highway Code rule 300.)

explanation: Adapt your driving to the appropriate type and condition of road. Do not treat speed limits as a target. Take the road and traffic conditions into account. Where there are junctions, be prepared for road users emerging. (Highway Code rule 146.)
